items.prompt: In product management, what does the term MVP stand for?

options.label: Most Valuable Process
Minimal Variable Plan
Minimum Viable Product
Maximum Value Proposition

rubric: MVP means Minimum Viable Product: the smallest version that tests the core idea with real users.
Distractors mix up similar-sounding business terms.

items.prompt: Which short format describes a requirement from the user's point of view, such as "As a shopper, I want to save items so that I can buy them later"?

options.label: User story
Balance sheet
Org chart
Test log

rubric: A user story captures who wants what and why.
Other options are business or technical documents that do not describe user needs.

items.prompt: The RICE prioritisation framework scores each idea on which four factors?

options.label: Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort
Revenue, Impact, Cost, Experience
Risk, Income, Confidence, Effort
Reach, Interest, Complexity, Timing

rubric: RICE stands for Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort.
Distractors use plausible business words that are not part of the framework.

items.prompt: What is a product roadmap?

options.label: A detailed schedule of each engineer's daily tasks and deadlines
A list of bugs found during testing, ranked by severity
A record of past sales by region, used to forecast revenue
A high-level plan of where the product is heading over time

rubric: A roadmap is a high-level view of direction and planned work over time.
The task-schedule distractor confuses a roadmap with a detailed project plan.

items.prompt: In product work, what is a stakeholder?

options.label: An investor who funds the company and expects returns
Anyone with an interest in or influence over the product
An engineer who builds the product and maintains its code
A customer who pays for the product and uses it regularly

rubric: Stakeholders include anyone affected by or able to influence the product.
Distractors narrow the term to a single group.

items.prompt: Which of these are usual responsibilities of a product manager? Select all that apply.

options.label: Writing requirements such as user stories
Setting priorities for what the team builds next
Writing all production code personally
Running the company payroll process
Aligning stakeholders on the product plan

rubric: PMs prioritise, write requirements and align stakeholders.
Payroll and writing all code belong to other roles.

items.prompt: A product manager keeps one ordered list of features, bugs and improvements the team could work on. The most important items are at the top, and the team pulls work from it. What is this list called?

options.label: Release note
Product roadmap summary
Product backlog
Requirements sign-off sheet

rubric: The ordered list of possible work is the product backlog.
Release notes describe what already shipped.

items.prompt: Why do product teams write acceptance criteria for a feature?

options.label: To state the conditions that mark a feature as done
To record which engineer is responsible for fixing each bug found
To set the price that customers will pay for the feature at launch
To list the marketing channels that will be used to promote it

rubric: Acceptance criteria give a shared definition of done.
Other options describe unrelated documents.

items.prompt: Which of these is an outcome rather than an output?

options.label: Fewer customers abandoning checkout after the change
Writing and publishing the release notes for version 2
Completing ten new features by the end of the quarter
Shipping the redesigned checkout page to all users

rubric: An outcome is a change in customer behaviour or results.
Shipped features and documents are outputs, which a team can deliver without achieving any change.

items.prompt: Why must a product manager prioritise work instead of building every requested feature?

options.label: Engineers do their best work on one feature at a time, so they refuse parallel work
Time and people are limited, so the team must pick what delivers most value
A roadmap is only readable if it lists a few items, so extra requests get cut
Customers distrust products with many features, so fewer features always sell better

rubric: Prioritisation exists because capacity is limited.
Distractors give invented rules or false claims.

items.prompt: Which requirement is a non-functional requirement?

options.label: Admins can delete user accounts after confirming a warning
Users can export a monthly sales report as a CSV file
Pages must load in under two seconds for most users
Users can reset their password using a link sent by email

rubric: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as speed, not specific actions.
The other options describe what users can do, so they are functional.

items.prompt: Why should a product manager involve engineers early when shaping a new idea?

options.label: To get feasibility and effort input before promises are made
To hand over ownership of product strategy to the engineering team
To make sure designers are not needed later in the project
To replace written requirements with verbal agreements on scope

rubric: Early engineering input exposes cost and feasibility before commitments are made.
Distractors assume engineering replaces other responsibilities.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why a roadmap is often framed around problems or outcomes instead of fixed feature dates? Select all that apply.

options.label: Early estimates are uncertain, so firm dates are often missed
It stops engineers from having to estimate work
It removes the need to talk to stakeholders
It leaves room to change solutions as the team learns from customers

rubric: Outcome-based roadmaps accept uncertainty and allow learning.
They do not remove stakeholder communication or estimation.

items.prompt: A sales rep asks the product manager to build a custom feature because one large prospect requested it. The PM has not heard this need from other customers. What is the best way to understand and respond to this request?

options.label: Check whether the underlying problem affects many users
Add it to the roadmap with a firm date to keep sales and the prospect happy
Build it first, since requests from the largest customers outrank other work
Reject it, since requests passed on by sales are never valid product input

rubric: A single request is a signal to investigate, not an automatic commitment.
Distractors either obey or dismiss the request without evidence.

items.prompt: Which of these is a customer problem statement rather than a proposed solution?

options.label: Add a bulk-upload button to the invoice page for faster entry
Redesign the invoice dashboard so it looks more modern and clean
Small-business owners lose two hours weekly matching invoices by hand
Integrate the app with the most popular accounting software tools

rubric: A problem statement describes the user's pain and its cost without prescribing a fix.
The other options are solutions that skip the problem, which is a common habit.

items.prompt: Why do many teams use a Now/Next/Later roadmap instead of one that gives a fixed date to every item?

options.label: It shows priorities and direction while admitting later items may change as the team learns
It replaces the backlog, so engineers can build from the roadmap without detailed requirements for each item
It lets the team skip estimating work, because with no dates on the roadmap the team never needs sizing
It gives stakeholders a firm commitment that every Later item will ship within the next twelve months

rubric: Now/Next/Later communicates direction and priority without false precision about later work.
Distractors treat it as a way to avoid estimates or as a hidden commitment.

items.prompt: In the RICE prioritisation model, what does the 'Reach' factor represent?

options.label: People affected in a given time period
How confident the team is in its estimates
How many person-weeks the work needs
How much each affected person benefits

rubric: Reach is the number of people or events affected in a set period.
Confidence, Impact and Effort are the other RICE factors that learners confuse it with.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of acceptance criteria on a user story?

options.label: To estimate how many story points the work will take
To describe the feature to customers in launch messaging
To state the conditions the story must meet to count as done
To list the tasks each engineer will do during the sprint

rubric: Acceptance criteria define when a story is done and can be verified.
Distractors confuse them with task breakdowns, estimates or marketing copy.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes a minimum viable product (MVP)?

options.label: The complete planned feature set trimmed until it fits the deadline
The smallest version that lets real users test the riskiest assumption
A clickable prototype shown only to executives to gain sign-off
A rough first release the team plans to leave unchanged afterward

rubric: An MVP exists to learn from real users by testing the riskiest assumption cheaply.
Distractors treat it as a low-quality final product, a cut-down scope or an internal demo.

items.prompt: Which of these are outcome measures (changes in user behaviour or results) rather than output measures (amount of work done)? Select all that apply.

options.label: Share of new users who finish a first project rises from 30% to 45%
Checkout support tickets fall by 25%
Story points completed per sprint
Number of features shipped this quarter
Number of design mockups produced

rubric: Outcomes describe changes in user behaviour or results.
Features shipped, points completed and mockups made only count work produced.

items.prompt: A stakeholder writes a ticket reading 'Make search better.' The engineers ask what to build, and the designer asks how success will be judged. You are the PM and must explain why the ticket is not ready for the team. What is the main issue with it?

options.label: It is a problem statement, so it should be turned into a solution before discussion
It is fine as written because engineers decide what better means on their own
It lacks a technical design, which the PM must write before engineers start
It gives no user problem or measurable target, so nobody can tell when it is done

rubric: The ticket has no user problem, goal or acceptance criteria, so done is undefined.
Distractors push the PM to write technical designs or assume vague requests are fine.

items.prompt: A backlog item is estimated at Reach 2,000 users per quarter, Impact 2, Confidence 50% and Effort 4 person-months. Using RICE = (Reach x Impact x Confidence) / Effort, what RICE score should it get?
rubric: 2,000 x 2 x 0.5 = 2,000, divided by 4 gives 500.
1,000 results from ignoring Confidence and 2,000 from ignoring Effort.

items.prompt: Your team wants to let shoppers store payment details for later purchases. Which is a well-formed user story for it?

options.label: As a returning shopper, I want to save my card so that I can check out faster
As a developer, I want a card vault table so that payment data is stored safely
Build a save-card feature for the checkout page in the next sprint
The system shall store card details securely using tokenisation at checkout

rubric: A user story names a user, a need and a benefit.
Other options are a technical task, a system requirement and a work order.

items.prompt: A ticketing app launches in six weeks and is legally required to show cancellation terms before purchase. Under MoSCoW, how should showing the terms be classed for this launch?

options.label: Must have
Won't have
Could have
Should have

rubric: A legal requirement without which the launch cannot proceed is a Must have.
Should and Could understate a non-negotiable constraint.

items.prompt: On a value-versus-effort grid, Idea A is high value and high effort, Idea B high value and low effort, Idea C low value and low effort, and Idea D low value and high effort. Which should be scheduled first?

options.label: Idea D
Idea B
Idea A
Idea C

rubric: High value with low effort is the quick win and goes first.
Idea C is tempting because it is cheap, but its value is low.

items.prompt: In one month, 5,000 people visit a pricing page, 400 start a free trial and 100 of those trial users become paying customers. What is the trial-to-paid conversion rate?
rubric: Conversion from trial to paid is 100 / 400 = 25%.
2% uses visitors as the base, and 8% is the visitor-to-trial rate.

items.prompt: You are writing acceptance criteria for a 'user can reset their password' story. Which criteria are testable as written? Select all that apply.

options.label: A new password under eight characters is rejected with an error message
The page uses friendly wording that customers enjoy
The reset link stops working after 24 hours
A reset link is emailed within one minute of the request
The reset process feels quick and easy for users

rubric: Testable criteria state observable, specific conditions such as a time limit or an error.
'Feels easy' and 'friendly wording' are subjective and cannot be verified pass or fail.

items.prompt: Your quarter's roadmap focuses on onboarding. A sales lead asks you to add a custom export feature for one large prospect and calls it urgent. Your team scores every request with the same prioritisation method. What is the best next step?

options.label: Decline right away because the quarter's roadmap is already committed
Put it at the top of the roadmap because a large prospect's deal is at stake
Ask engineering to squeeze it in beside onboarding work without scoring
Clarify the underlying problem, then score it against the same criteria

rubric: Understanding the problem and scoring the request consistently lets it compete fairly with other work.
Automatically accepting, refusing or sneaking in the request skips the prioritisation process.

items.prompt: A team scores a feature using RICE = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) / Effort. Reach is 3000 users per quarter, Impact is 2, Confidence is 80% and Effort is 6 person-months. What is its RICE score?
rubric: 2000 × 2 × 0.5 = 2000, divided by 4 gives 500.
1000 forgets to divide by effort after applying confidence; 4000 forgets confidence.

items.prompt: You are writing a user story for search in an inventory tool. Which acceptance criterion can be tested as written?

options.label: Searching a SKU returns matching items within 2 seconds for 95% of queries on a 10,000-item catalogue
Search feels fast and responsive to warehouse managers across all typical inventory catalogue sizes
Search quality is at least as good as the leading competitor's search in comparable inventory tools
Search is built on a modern indexing approach so results stay relevant as the catalogue grows

rubric: A testable criterion has a measurable threshold and defined conditions.
Distractors are vague, implementation-focused or relative, so no pass/fail check exists.

items.prompt: A team delivers 30 story points per sprint. Four sprints remain before launch, and 20% of capacity is reserved for bug fixes and support. How many points of roadmap features can you plan?
rubric: 30 × 4 = 120 total; 80% of that is 96.
120 ignores the reserve; 24 is the reserve itself, not the remainder.

items.prompt: Of 10,000 monthly visitors, 20% sign up, 40% of sign-ups activate and 50% of activated users pay. Activation improves from 40% to 50%, other rates unchanged. How many paying customers result per month?
rubric: 400 is the old baseline; 450 and 600 come from adding rather than multiplying rates.

items.prompt: Launch is fixed in 8 weeks. Capacity fits only 6 of 10 candidate items. One item is a legal requirement for the target market; another is a popular but non-blocking request. How do you apply MoSCoW?

options.label: Legal item is Should because it can be patched after launch; the popular request is Must
Neither is Must until engineering estimates every item, since priority is decided by effort
Both are Must because customers and regulators both expect them to be present on launch day
Legal item is Must; the popular request is Should or Could, ranked against remaining capacity

rubric: Must means the launch fails or is illegal without it; popularity alone does not qualify.
Marking everything Must ignores the capacity limit; effort does not define priority.

items.prompt: You are writing requirements for a 'saved payment methods' feature. Which belong in the requirements document? Select all that apply.

options.label: The database library engineers must use to store card tokens
Exact pixel spacing for the card list, decided without design input
Acceptance criteria covering what happens when a saved card has expired
A list of non-goals, such as not supporting bank transfers in this release
A success metric, such as checkout completion rate for returning customers

rubric: Requirements state the problem, success measures, scope boundaries and testable behaviour.
Library choice and pixel layout belong to engineering and design, not the PM's requirements.

items.prompt: A sales lead asks you to build a custom export for one enterprise customer worth 8% of revenue. Your quarter is fully planned, and 2 of 30 interviewed customers mention a similar need. Using your team's prioritisation framework, what is the best next step?

options.label: Score it with the same criteria as planned items, then decide what it would displace and explain why
Decline it outright because only 2 of 30 interviewees mentioned it, so it cannot justify any effort
Ask engineering to fit it in alongside current work, since sprint estimates usually contain enough slack
Add it to the quarter at once because the customer's large revenue share outweighs the thin interview evidence

rubric: Apply the framework consistently and make the trade-off against committed work explicit.
Other options skip scoring, ignore revenue context, or hide the cost in assumed slack.

items.prompt: After launch, 60% of users who see a new 'Automations' entry point click it, but only 8% finish setup. Funnel data shows 55% abandon at step 3, which asks for API credentials. What is the best-supported diagnosis?

options.label: Demand is absent, since most users who click never finish setup anyway
Step 3 is a friction point for non-technical users, so test simplifying or deferring it
The entry point misleads users into clicking, so its label should be rewritten first
Awareness is too low, so more promotion of the entry point is the priority fix

rubric: The data localises the loss at step 3 after strong click-through.
Awareness and misleading-label explanations conflict with the 60% click rate.

items.prompt: Engineering keeps missing roadmap dates and morale is dropping. The roadmap lists exact quarter-end dates for every item, including ones still in discovery. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: Dates were not repeated in sprint planning, so engineers forgot the quarter commitments
The roadmap has too few items, so teams lack enough work to stay focused on
Engineers estimate too optimistically, so padding every estimate by 50% would remove the problem
Uncertain discovery work was shown as committed dates, so the roadmap promised certainty it lacked

rubric: Dates on unvalidated work create commitments the team cannot reliably meet.
Padding and reminders treat symptoms rather than the false certainty in the roadmap.

items.prompt: A campaign lifted sign-ups 30%, yet 30-day retention fell from 40% to 31%. Which analysis step best tests the likely cause?

options.label: Compare retention by acquisition channel, since campaign users may be lower intent
Compare total sign-ups before and after the campaign to confirm that the lift was real and not seasonal
Survey only retained users about what they value most, then fix whatever the others are likely missing
Roll back the latest release, since retention drops are usually caused by recent code changes

rubric: Segmenting by channel tests for a cohort mix shift that lowers blended retention.
Surveying only survivors and blind rollback do not isolate the cause.

items.prompt: RICE ranks feature A first and feature B fifth. Engineering says A cannot ship without B's new data model. What does this imply for prioritisation?

options.label: B must now be ranked first, since anything that blocks another item goes first
The ranking stands, since dependencies are for engineers to manage and not for scoring
A's effort should include B's work, which may lower A's score and change the ranking
Feature A should be dropped, since any dependency means the feature is too risky

rubric: The true cost of A includes the prerequisite work, so its score must be recalculated.
Other options ignore the cost, over-correct mechanically, or reject A without analysis.

items.prompt: For three sprints, about 40% of stories carry over. Retros show design specs for those stories changed mid-sprint, after engineers had started. Which process step is most likely faulty?

options.label: Velocity is not tracked per person, so individuals are not accountable for finishing work
Stories enter sprints before design is settled, so a definition of ready is missing or ignored
Engineers do not hold daily standups, so blockers are not raised until it is too late
Sprints are too short for the team's capacity, so lengthening them would fix carry-over

rubric: The evidence points to unsettled inputs at sprint start, which a definition of ready prevents.
Sprint length, standups and individual velocity do not address mid-sprint spec changes.

items.prompt: Which findings make a team's A/B test result unreliable? Select all that apply.

options.label: The test was stopped on day two when the variant first reached significance
Of 12 metrics tracked, only the one that favoured the variant was reported
Users were assigned to control and variant by a 50/50 random split
The test ran two full weeks, covering two complete weekly usage cycles

rubric: Early stopping and selective metric reporting inflate false positives.
Full weekly cycles and random assignment are sound practice.

items.prompt: Churn is rising. In interviews, churned customers say they wanted better reporting, and the team plans a dashboard. Usage data shows 80% of churned accounts never invited a second user, while retained accounts average four users. What is the strongest analysis?

options.label: Interview statements are direct evidence of what customers need, so the dashboard should go ahead as the main churn fix and usage data can confirm it later
Both findings carry equal weight and neither can be ranked, so build the dashboard and invite features together to cover both possible causes at once
Reporting may be a stated reason, but low team adoption predicts churn better, so test invite-driving onboarding first
Usage data only shows correlation, not cause, so it should be set aside in favour of what churned customers say they wanted when they left

rubric: Behavioural data on team adoption can reveal a cause that stated reasons miss; test it cheaply first.
Other options trust stated wants over behaviour, dismiss the data, or avoid prioritising.

items.prompt: A new onboarding flow has 60% drop-off at step 3, where users invite a teammate to approve data access. Interviews show most users are individual contributors without admin rights. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: The step 3 screen is cluttered, so users cannot find the invite button quickly and abandon the flow
Users lack motivation because the product's value has not yet been explained to them before this step
The flow has too many steps overall, so fatigue builds and users leave at the midpoint of the flow
The step needs an approver the user cannot act on alone, so progress stalls outside the product

rubric: Interviews show users lack admin rights, so the step blocks them on a third party.
Distractors blame UI, motivation or length, which the evidence does not support.

items.prompt: Five enterprise prospects each ask for a custom Excel export. Discovery calls reveal all five use it to reconcile data with finance's month-end close. What is the best analysis of these requests?

options.label: The requests reflect sales pressure more than need, so they should be discounted until usage data confirms them
The requests show the product lacks reporting, so a full reporting suite is the implied requirement
The shared job is month-end reconciliation, so the export is one possible solution among several
Five consistent requests confirm Excel export is the right solution, since demand is steady across accounts

rubric: Separating the underlying job from the requested solution keeps options open.
Distractors accept the solution as given, dismiss real signal, or over-generalise to a large suite.

items.prompt: After a paid campaign, signups rose 30% but activated users and revenue stayed flat. Which explanation is best supported and should be investigated first?

options.label: The campaign brought a lower-intent cohort, so activation per signup fell and offset the volume gain
The activation flow broke during the campaign, blocking the users who would normally have activated
Paid users are always lower quality, so the channel should be cut immediately without further analysis
Revenue lags signups, so flat revenue is expected and cohort differences need no examination

rubric: Flat activation with higher signups points to a change in cohort mix, which cohort analysis can test.
Distractors assume a break, ignore the signal, or jump to a blanket conclusion.

items.prompt: A RICE ranking puts a notification redesign first. Reach was set to all 200k monthly users, yet analytics show only 8k users have notifications enabled. Which input most distorts the ranking?

options.label: Reach counts users who can never be affected by the change, inflating the score by a large factor
Confidence was set too low, which unfairly penalised the redesign against competing items
Impact was scored too high, because redesigns rarely move retention as much as new features
Effort was underestimated, because design work is usually harder to size than engineering work

rubric: Reach should cover users the change touches; 8k versus 200k is a 25x overstatement.
Other inputs may be imperfect but the data contradicts only Reach.

items.prompt: Engineering estimates are accurate, yet three sprints in a row ended with 30% of committed work unfinished. Logs show about four unplanned items per sprint added after escalations from sales and support. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The team commits to more than its real capacity because it plans at its best-case sprint velocity rather than its average
Stories are too large to finish within one sprint, so work routinely carries over and is never fully completed on time
The team lacks velocity discipline and needs a larger buffer in each sprint to absorb normal variation in delivery
Escalations bypass prioritisation and displace committed work, so capacity goes to unplanned items

rubric: Accurate estimates plus regular unplanned additions point to displacement of committed work.
Distractors contradict the stated accuracy or treat a process leak as a sizing problem.

items.prompt: Which observations suggest a roadmap has drifted into a feature list rather than connecting work to outcomes? Select all that apply.

options.label: Nobody can say what would be stopped if a shipped item showed no impact
Some items are labelled as bets to be validated before commitment
Stakeholders judge roadmap success by the share of items delivered on time
Items are grouped into Now, Next and Later with less detail further out
Each item has a ship date but no target metric or customer problem attached

rubric: Missing outcomes, output-based success and no stop criteria mark a feature list.
Horizon grouping and labelled bets are signs of an outcome-oriented roadmap.

items.prompt: An A/B test of a new checkout shows +4% overall conversion. Desktop rose 9% and mobile fell 3%. Mobile is 70% of control traffic but only 40% of variant traffic because assignment was uneven by device. What should the PM conclude?

options.label: The mobile loss is noise, since the overall result is positive and reached statistical significance
Uneven device assignment confounds the overall lift, so check the test setup before deciding
The overall lift is valid because randomisation averages out segment differences between the two arms
Desktop gains outweigh the mobile loss, so ship the variant to desktop only and drop mobile

rubric: A device mix imbalance between arms means the arms are not comparable, so the topline is unreliable.
Distractors trust the topline or segment results without addressing the broken assignment.

items.prompt: A 6-person team must add SSO for two signed enterprise deals due in 8 weeks. Building it takes about 7 weeks and halts core roadmap work. A vendor integration takes 2 weeks, costs a moderate yearly fee, and supports the needed protocols. Criteria: meet the deadline, protect the core roadmap, accept moderate recurring cost. Which is best?

options.label: Integrate the vendor, because it meets the date and protects the core roadmap at an acceptable cost
Ask both customers to delay, because a custom build is the only way to satisfy their needs
Build a reduced in-house version, because partial SSO would satisfy the contracts in less time
Build in-house, because owning the capability avoids a recurring fee and vendor dependency

rubric: The vendor option is the only one meeting all three stated criteria.
Distractors ignore the roadmap criterion or invent unsupported assumptions about the contracts.

items.prompt: Which weakness in a draft PRD most threatens delivery of the intended outcome?

options.label: The PRD does not specify button colours or spacing, so the designer must make visual decisions alone during build
Success criteria read 'improve the experience' with no threshold, so no one can judge when scope is enough
The PRD lists explicit non-goals, which restricts engineering's freedom to propose alternatives once planning starts
The PRD runs to four pages, which is too much for engineers to read in full before sprint planning begins

rubric: Without measurable success criteria, scope and trade-offs cannot be settled.
Visual details, non-goals and length are routine and do not block delivery.

items.prompt: A seed-stage team has 20 customers and no usage baselines. Criteria: learn quickly and avoid false precision in prioritising. Which approach is best?

options.label: Build what the largest customer asks for, since revenue concentration signals real demand
Score items with RICE using careful estimates, since explicit comparison helps even with rough inputs
Wait for three months of analytics, so scoring inputs rest on observed data rather than guesses
Rank by riskiest assumption and run cheap tests, since formulas would rest on guessed numbers

rubric: With no baselines, testing the riskiest assumptions yields learning faster than scoring guesses.
Distractors give false precision, over-weight one customer, or delay learning.

items.prompt: A 20% price rise for existing customers is planned next month. Criteria: address first the risk with the largest harm that is hardest to reverse. Which risk should be addressed first?

options.label: High-value accounts may churn on learning of the rise without notice, and lost accounts rarely return
Support tickets will spike, which can be handled with temporary staffing and macros
Competitors may copy the new pricing tiers, which can be answered later with packaging changes
Finance forecasts may be off in the first quarter, which can be corrected in the next cycle

rubric: Churn of key accounts is the most severe and least reversible risk.
The other risks are real but recoverable after launch.

items.prompt: A two-sided marketplace needs a north-star metric. Criteria: reflect value to both sides, resist gaming, and lead revenue. Which is the best choice?

options.label: Number of active listings, since a larger supply of listings predicts how much buyers will find and buy
Total registered users, since growth on both sides shows a rising network size and future liquidity
Gross merchandise value per month, since it tracks revenue directly and is simple to report to the board
Weekly transactions both sides confirm as satisfactory, since they show real matched value

rubric: Confirmed completed transactions capture both sides, are hard to game and lead revenue.
Distractors measure size, supply only, or lagging revenue.

items.prompt: A large customer demands a custom feature. Which are valid reasons for the PM to decline or reshape the request? Select all that apply.

options.label: An existing capability or integration can meet the need at acceptable effort for the customer
It serves one account's workflow and its upkeep would slow work for the wider segment
The customer is large, so the request is probably only a negotiating tactic
Engineering called it hard, so it should be rejected without further discussion
It conflicts with the chosen positioning and the revenue at stake does not justify shifting it

rubric: Valid reasons rest on segment fit, existing alternatives and strategy.
Assuming bad faith or rejecting on difficulty alone is not a reasoned judgement.

items.prompt: A launch is tied to a conference in 5 days. Beta shows exports silently drop rows for about 2% of accounts with files over 50k rows; the fix needs 3 weeks. Criteria: avoid data-integrity harm, keep the commitment, preserve trust. What is the best decision?

options.label: Launch on time with large exports blocked and a visible warning, fix scheduled, so no data is silently lost
Launch on time and list the issue in release notes, because 2% of accounts is small
Launch on time and patch quietly later, because announcing the flaw would hurt the conference message
Delay the whole launch 3 weeks, because any known defect should block release

rubric: Blocking large exports removes silent data loss while keeping the date and honesty.
Distractors sacrifice the date needlessly, accept silent loss, or hide the defect.

items.prompt: A team ranks its backlog by RICE score. A platform migration scores low because its direct Reach is small, yet it unblocks three high-scoring features. Which critique of the scoring is strongest?

options.label: RICE should drop Effort, because engineering estimates are unreliable and bias the ranking against large items
RICE's Confidence term double-counts risk, so the migration should be rescored with Confidence set to 100%
RICE only suits consumer products, so the migration should be ranked by the CEO's stated preference instead
RICE scores items independently, so it undervalues enablers whose value arrives through the work they unlock

rubric: RICE treats each item in isolation, so dependency and enabler value is missed.
Distractors misattribute the flaw to Effort or Confidence rather than to independence of items.

items.prompt: A two-sided marketplace needs one North Star metric. Criteria: reflects value to both buyers and sellers, moves before revenue does, and is hard to inflate with promotions. Which candidate fits best?

options.label: Average NPS across both sides, since satisfaction predicts later revenue and discounts cannot buy it
Gross merchandise value per month, since it moves before revenue does and rises whenever either side transacts more
Registered users per month, since growth on both sides is the precondition for any transaction happening
Buyer-seller pairs completing a repeat transaction within 60 days, since repeats show both sides got value

rubric: Repeat matches signal value for both sides, lead revenue and resist promotional inflation.
GMV and signups are easily inflated; NPS is not tied to both sides' actual behaviour.

items.prompt: Sales needs dates to close enterprise deals. Discovery shows two of five roadmap items carry high technical uncertainty. Criteria: keep credibility with customers, preserve room to learn, avoid sandbagging. Which approach is best?

options.label: Give sales the engineers' optimistic estimates as targets, since stretch dates motivate the team to deliver
Drop dates entirely and share only themes, since any date will eventually be read by customers as a promise
Publish dated commitments for all five items with a 30% buffer, so sales always has a safe date to quote
Commit to dates for the three well-understood items and show the other two as Next with stated confidence

rubric: Committing only where uncertainty is low keeps credibility while preserving learning room.
Blanket buffers sandbag, optimistic targets erode trust, and no dates fails the sales need.

items.prompt: A checkout redesign shows +6% conversion after 4 days of a planned 14-day A/B test. The lift is concentrated among returning users and is shrinking each day. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Keep the test running as planned and segment by user type, since a decaying lift suggests novelty
Ship now, because the lift is positive and statistically significant on the days measured so far, and waiting risks losing revenue
Stop the test and discard the design, because a lift that shrinks each day proves the original effect was only noise
Extend the test until the lift is significant again, because ending at the planned length cuts off winners that need more time

rubric: A decaying lift concentrated in returning users points to novelty; the pre-planned duration and segmentation test it.
Early shipping and extending until significant both ignore peeking and novelty bias.

items.prompt: A six-engineer team focused on its core matching algorithm needs login and identity management within 8 weeks. It is not a differentiator, and security risk is high. Which option best meets these criteria?

options.label: Build a minimal version now and replace it later, since early security shortcuts are cheap to repay
Build in-house, because owning authentication avoids vendor lock-in and gives full control over security
Buy the cheapest option available, since non-differentiating capabilities should be minimised on cost alone
Buy a managed service behind a thin interface, since it is non-differentiating and frees the team for matching

rubric: Buying a proven service for a non-differentiating, high-risk capability fits the time and focus criteria; an interface limits lock-in.
Building diverts the core team, and picking on price alone ignores security risk.

items.prompt: A team plans to prioritise features by how many customers request them. Which criticisms of this approach are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Volume ranking is sound as long as requests are tallied weekly rather than quarterly
Customers describe solutions, so counts can hide that different requests share one underlying problem
Request counts are meaningless, so interview data should be the only input to prioritisation
Frequent requests for existing capabilities may signal a discoverability problem, not a missing feature
Request volume reflects the loudest segments, which may not be the most valuable or strategic ones

rubric: Volume is biased by segment, conflates solutions with problems and can mask discoverability issues.
Rejecting all request data or fixing tally frequency are overcorrections that miss the real flaws.

items.prompt: Your CEO wants a flashy AI feature this quarter to match a competitor. Retention data shows 40% of new users churn in week one because of onboarding friction, and the team can ship only one major item. Criteria: protect strategy, keep executive trust, stay evidence-based. Which response is best?

options.label: Ship the AI feature as requested, since the CEO holds the strategic context and pushing back would cost the team its credibility
Split the team evenly between both efforts so neither stakeholder is disappointed, and report progress on each every month
Refuse the AI feature and fix onboarding, since retention data outranks any executive request and the team must protect users
Show the churn cost against the competitive risk, propose a small AI spike beside onboarding, and agree on a decision metric

rubric: It uses evidence to reframe the trade-off, limits the competitive risk cheaply and keeps the CEO involved in the decision.
Capitulating or refusing outright damages trust or strategy; an even split dilutes both efforts.

items.prompt: A product has about 1,500 weekly active users. The team must decide within four weeks whether a new onboarding flow improves 90-day retention. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: Ship to everyone and compare retention with last quarter, since the sample is then as large as possible
Run a standard A/B test on 90-day retention and wait for significance, however long it takes to reach
Survey 50 users on satisfaction with the new flow, since 90-day retention cannot be measured in four weeks
Randomise the flow and measure an activation event shown to predict 90-day retention, plus 8 user sessions

rubric: A validated leading proxy in a randomised comparison, with qualitative support, fits the traffic and time limits.
Waiting breaks the deadline, before/after comparisons are confounded, and satisfaction is not a validated predictor.

items.prompt: A PRD for a bulk-export feature lists user stories, acceptance criteria, mockups and a launch date. Which missing element most weakens the team's ability to learn whether it worked and to react if it did not?

options.label: A success metric with a baseline and threshold, plus a defined trigger for iteration or rollback
A detailed engineering task breakdown with story-point estimates assigned to each named developer
A list of every UI edge case, including the exact error-message copy written for each possible state
A comparison table of at least five direct and indirect competitors and how each handles export

rubric: Without a baseline, threshold and decision trigger, the team cannot judge success or act on failure.
The other items add detail but do not enable outcome judgement.

items.prompt: A legacy API brings in 20% of revenue and must be sunset within 9 months to cut costs. Fifteen enterprise customers have custom integrations, and engineering can support only one migration tool. Which plan meets all constraints?

options.label: Build bespoke migrations for each of the 15 customers in sequence, then announce the sunset when all are done
Announce early with a date, build one compatibility layer and migration tool, and assist the top accounts
Announce a hard shutdown at month nine and publish migration docs, leaving each customer to port itself
Keep the legacy API indefinitely for enterprise accounts and sunset it only for self-serve users

rubric: Early notice, a single tool and targeted help protect revenue within the deadline and tooling limit.
Hard shutdown risks churn, indefinite support misses the cost goal, and bespoke work breaks the one-tool constraint.

items.prompt: SMB customers want simplicity and enterprise customers want configurability. Constraints: one codebase, no forked UX, both segments retained. Which product design meets them?

options.label: Create separate enterprise and SMB apps on two codebases so each can be optimised independently
Layer progressive disclosure: simple defaults for SMB, with admin-level configuration behind permissions
Build every configuration option and expose all of them by default so enterprise needs are met first
Remove configuration entirely and favour SMB, since the larger segment by count sets product direction

rubric: Progressive disclosure serves both segments in one codebase and one UX.
Other options sacrifice a segment or violate the single-codebase constraint.

items.prompt: Design a key result for a team accountable for activation. Constraints: it must measure an outcome rather than output, sit within the team's influence, and include a guard against gaming. Which meets all three?

options.label: Ship five onboarding features this quarter, with no guardrail since shipping is directly verifiable
Improve onboarding satisfaction as scored by the PM's own judgement, with weekly team retrospectives as guardrail
Raise week-one activation from 32% to 40%, with support tickets and 30-day retention required not to decline
Increase company revenue by 15%, with a monthly executive review of the revenue forecast as the guardrail

rubric: A baseline-to-target activation outcome with guardrail metrics is controllable and resists gaming.
Other options are outputs, too distant from the team, or subjective.

items.prompt: You must write a decision memo asking leadership to fund a new product bet. Which elements make it a complete, decidable case? Select all that apply.

options.label: Options considered, including doing nothing, with the reason the recommendation beats them
Only the upside scenario, to keep the request short and focused
The problem evidence and target segment, stated so leadership can challenge them
A full list of every feature screen so leadership can approve the design details
Key assumptions with the cheapest test for each and the signal that would stop the bet

rubric: A decidable memo exposes evidence, alternatives and the assumptions and stop signals.
Screen detail is not a funding decision input, and upside-only framing hides risk.

items.prompt: Your largest customer's contract requires a compliance feature by 30 June, 12 weeks away. Engineering estimates 8 to 16 weeks because scope is uncertain. The team also owes a growth experiment. Which plan meets the date while limiting risk?

options.label: Commit to the full scope for 30 June and add engineers late to compress the 16-week upper estimate
Pause the growth experiment and build everything in parallel, cutting scope only if the date is clearly missed
Tell the customer the date cannot be met, then negotiate after the full scope is finished in 16 weeks
Cut scope to the contractual minimum, spike the uncertain parts first, and set a checkpoint to decide trade-offs

rubric: Minimum contractual scope, early de-risking and a checkpoint fit the fixed date and uncertain estimate.
Adding people late, ignoring the date, or deferring scope cuts all leave the deadline at risk.
